Linear Search.problem: Return the first zero-based index matching target, or -1.
Linear Search.approach: Check entries from left to right. A match is first because all earlier entries were already checked.
Linear Search.pitfalls: Empty input returns -1. An unsorted array cannot use binary search safely.

Largest Element.problem: Return the maximum of a nonempty array.
Largest Element.approach: Initialize from a real entry, then maintain the largest processed value.
Largest Element.pitfalls: Starting best at zero is wrong for all-negative inputs.
Largest Element.alternatives: Sorting takes O(n log n) and may mutate input unnecessarily.

Second Largest Element.problem: Return the second largest DISTINCT value, or OptionalInt.empty if it does not exist.
Second Largest Element.approach: Maintain largest and second-largest distinct processed values. A new maximum demotes the old maximum; an intermediate distinct value only updates second.
Second Largest Element.trace: 4 sets first; duplicate 4 changes nothing; 2 sets second; -1 changes nothing.
Second Largest Element.pitfalls: A sentinel like -1 is ambiguous. MIN_VALUE can be a valid second largest.

Maximum Consecutive Ones.problem: For a binary array return the longest consecutive run of ones.
Maximum Consecutive Ones.approach: Keep the length of the suffix consisting only of ones, reset on zero, and record the largest suffix length.
Maximum Consecutive Ones.pitfalls: Empty array returns zero; a non-one value is treated as a separator.

Left Rotate Array by One.problem: Rotate left by one in place.
Left Rotate Array by One.approach: Save the first value before shifting; place it at the last index.
Left Rotate Array by One.trace: Save 1, shift 2 and 3 left, append saved 1.
Left Rotate Array by One.pitfalls: Empty and singleton arrays need no change.

Left Rotate Array by K Places.problem: Rotate left by k in place. Negative k rotates right; normalize by length.
Left Rotate Array by K Places.approach: Split into A (first k) and B (rest). reverse(A), reverse(B), then reverse(all) gives BA, with internal order restored.
Left Rotate Array by K Places.pitfalls: Handle empty input before modulo. Math.floorMod supports negative k.
Left Rotate Array by K Places.alternatives: A temporary output array takes O(n) space. Repeating one-step rotation k times takes O(nk) time.

Move Zeros to End.problem: Move zeros to the end in place while preserving the order of nonzero entries.
Move Zeros to End.approach: Compact nonzero values into a prefix, then fill the remaining suffix with zeros. write never overtakes the read position.
Move Zeros to End.trace: write receives 1,3,2 at positions 0,1,2; fill positions 3,4 with zero.
Move Zeros to End.pitfalls: The enhanced loop is safe here because writes only affect earlier/current positions.
Move Zeros to End.alternatives: A second array is a simpler O(n)-space approach.

Remove duplicates from sorted array.problem: For a nondecreasing array, return unique-prefix length and place distinct values in that prefix. Entries beyond the length are unspecified.
Remove duplicates from sorted array.approach: Adjacent equal values form one block; copy only the first of each block.
Remove duplicates from sorted array.trace: 1 copied, next 1 skipped; 2 copied, next 2 skipped; 3 copied.
Remove duplicates from sorted array.pitfalls: Input MUST be sorted; length zero is valid. Do not print the unused suffix.

Find missing number.problem: n distinct values from [0,n] contain exactly one missing value; return it.
Find missing number.approach: XOR all indices 0..n and all entries. Each present value appears twice and cancels, leaving the missing one.
Find missing number.pitfalls: Duplicates or values outside [0,n] violate the contract.
Find missing number.alternatives: Summation uses n*(n+1)/2 minus array sum, but widen before multiplication; XOR avoids that arithmetic overflow.

Union of two sorted arrays.problem: Return sorted distinct union of two nondecreasing arrays.
Union of two sorted arrays.approach: Two sorted fronts let us discard the smaller unmatched value for intersection, or emit the smaller available value for union. Each pointer only moves forward.
Union of two sorted arrays.trace: A=[1,2,2,4], B=[2,2,3]: equal fronts at the two occurrences of 2 contribute intersection; union emits every distinct value once.
Union of two sorted arrays.pitfalls: Intersection here uses multiplicity; adapt by suppressing equal outputs if the judge asks for set intersection. Both inputs must be sorted.

Intersection of two sorted arrays.problem: Return sorted multiset intersection (duplicates appear min(countA,countB) times).
Intersection of two sorted arrays.approach: Two sorted fronts let us discard the smaller unmatched value for intersection, or emit the smaller available value for union. Each pointer only moves forward.
Intersection of two sorted arrays.trace: A=[1,2,2,4], B=[2,2,3]: equal fronts at the two occurrences of 2 contribute intersection; union emits every distinct value once.
Intersection of two sorted arrays.pitfalls: Intersection here uses multiplicity; adapt by suppressing equal outputs if the judge asks for set intersection. Both inputs must be sorted.

Majority Element-I.problem: Return the value occurring more than floor(n/2) times, or empty if absent.
Majority Element-I.approach: Boyer-Moore cancels pairs of unequal values. A strict majority cannot be entirely cancelled. A second pass verifies the candidate.
Majority Element-I.trace: 2 gives vote 1, another 2 gives 2, 1 reduces to 1, final 2 gives 2; count is 3>2.
Majority Element-I.pitfalls: Verification is required unless existence is guaranteed. Empty input returns empty.
Majority Element-I.alternatives: HashMap counting uses expected O(n) time and O(n) space; sorting uses O(n log n) time.

Leaders in an Array.problem: A leader is STRICTLY greater than every value to its right. Return leaders in original order.
Leaders in an Array.approach: Scan from the right while maintaining the largest right-side value. A value is a leader exactly when it beats that maximum.
Leaders in an Array.complexity: O(n) time; O(number of leaders) output space.
Leaders in an Array.trace: From right: keep 2, keep 5, skip 3 and 4, keep 17, skip 16; reverse kept list.
Leaders in an Array.pitfalls: Some platforms use >= rather than >; this contract is strict. Long.MIN_VALUE allows Integer.MIN_VALUE to be a leader.
Leaders in an Array.alternatives: Brute force checks every right suffix in O(n²) time.

Rearrange array elements by sign.problem: Stable alternate nonnegative and negative values, starting nonnegative. If counts differ, append the remaining values. Return a new array.
Rearrange array elements by sign.approach: Split into stable sign lists, then weave them. Each sign list preserves its original relative order.
Rearrange array elements by sign.trace: pos=[3,1,2], neg=[-2,-5,-4]; weave the corresponding fronts.
Rearrange array elements by sign.pitfalls: Zero is classified as nonnegative. Equal sign counts are not required.
Rearrange array elements by sign.alternatives: With exactly equal counts and no zero, write positives to even positions and negatives to odd positions in one pass.

Print the matrix in spiral manner.problem: Return clockwise spiral order of a rectangular matrix.
Print the matrix in spiral manner.approach: Visit top, right, bottom, left boundaries, then shrink them. Guard bottom and left traversals after shrinking to avoid duplicate visits in a single row or column.
Print the matrix in spiral manner.complexity: O(rows*cols) time and output space; O(1) auxiliary state.
Print the matrix in spiral manner.pitfalls: Ragged arrays are outside the contract. Empty rows/columns return empty.

Pascal's Triangle I.problem: Return an entry using ONE-based row and column coordinates.
Pascal's Triangle I.approach: Row r column c equals C(r-1,c-1). The multiplicative formula keeps exact intermediate binomial values.
Pascal's Triangle I.complexity: O(min(c-1,r-c)) BigInteger multiply/divide operations; storage grows with result bits.
Pascal's Triangle I.pitfalls: Do not mix one-based coordinates with zero-based combinatorial parameters.

Pascal's Triangle II.problem: Return the whole ONE-based row as exact BigIntegers.
Pascal's Triangle II.approach: Start from C(n,0)=1 and use C(n,k+1)=C(n,k)*(n-k)/(k+1). The division is exact.
Pascal's Triangle II.complexity: O(row) BigInteger arithmetic operations and O(row) output values; bit cost depends on row.
Pascal's Triangle II.pitfalls: row=1 returns [1]. Large rows overflow int/long, hence BigInteger.

Pascal's Triangle III.problem: Generate the first n rows, n>=0.
Pascal's Triangle III.approach: Boundary cells are one; each interior cell sums the two parents directly above it. Induction on row proves Pascal recurrence.
Pascal's Triangle III.complexity: O(n²) BigInteger additions; O(n²) output values, whose bit size grows with row.
Pascal's Triangle III.pitfalls: n=0 returns an empty list. Returned rows are separate objects.

Rotate matrix by 90 degrees.problem: Rotate a square matrix clockwise by 90 degrees in place.
Rotate matrix by 90 degrees.approach: Transpose maps (r,c) to (c,r); reversing each row then maps to (c,n-1-r), the clockwise position.
Rotate matrix by 90 degrees.pitfalls: Only transpose above the diagonal; transposing both halves would undo swaps. Rectangular matrices need a new differently shaped array.

Set Matrix Zeroes.problem: For every ORIGINAL zero, set its whole row and column to zero in place. Matrix is rectangular.
Set Matrix Zeroes.approach: Use first row/column as markers, while saving whether those original borders themselves need zeroing. Read all interior markers before overwriting the borders.
Set Matrix Zeroes.trace: Center zero marks a[1][0] and a[0][1]; interior pass zeros row 1 and column 1.
Set Matrix Zeroes.pitfalls: Zeroing immediately while discovering zeros propagates false zeros. Empty matrix is valid.
Set Matrix Zeroes.alternatives: A copy costs O(mn) space; separate row/column flags cost O(m+n) space.

Two Sum.problem: Return two distinct zero-based indices summing to target, or [-1,-1]. Any pair is acceptable.
Two Sum.approach: Before inserting current value, look for its complement among earlier entries. This guarantees different indices.
Two Sum.complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(n) space.
Two Sum.trace: At 2 look for 7 and store index 0; at 7 look for 2 and return [0,1].
Two Sum.pitfalls: Widen complement subtraction to long; repeated equal values need two positions.
Two Sum.alternatives: Nested pair enumeration takes O(n²) time and O(1) space. Sorting plus two pointers takes O(n log n) but needs index tracking.

3 Sum.problem: Return unique value triples with zero sum, using distinct indices. Input is not mutated.
3 Sum.approach: Sort a copy. Fix the first value, then move left/right based on sum. Sorted order proves that when sum is low, increasing left is the only useful direction. Skip equal fixed and endpoint values.
3 Sum.complexity: O(n²) time after sorting; O(n) copy plus result space.
3 Sum.pitfalls: Use long sum to avoid int overflow. Unique value triples differ from unique index triples.
3 Sum.alternatives: Enumerating all index triples takes O(n³), plus deduplication storage.

4 Sum.problem: Return unique sorted value quadruples summing to target, using four different indices.
4 Sum.approach: Fix two sorted positions, then solve two-sum on the suffix. Skip duplicates at both fixed positions and both moving endpoints.
4 Sum.complexity: O(n³) time, O(n) copy plus output storage.
4 Sum.trace: Fix -2,-1 -> need 3, giving 1,2; fix -2,0 -> need 2, giving 0,2.
4 Sum.pitfalls: Widen the FIRST addition. Casting a sum after int arithmetic is too late.
4 Sum.alternatives: Four nested loops take O(n⁴); pair-sum hashing can improve time with substantial duplicate/index bookkeeping and O(n²) storage.

Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's.problem: Sort an array containing only 0,1,2 in place.
Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's.approach: Dutch National Flag invariant: [0,low) zeros, [low,mid) ones, [mid,high] unknown, (high,n) twos. Every step shrinks the unknown region.
Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's.trace: A 2 swaps to the high boundary; recheck the incoming unknown value. A 0 swaps to low, a 1 simply advances mid.
Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's.pitfalls: Do not advance mid after swapping with high: the incoming element has not been classified.
Sort an array of 0's 1's and 2's.alternatives: Counting 0/1/2 then overwriting also takes O(n) time and O(1) space, but uses two passes.

Kadane's Algorithm.problem: Return the maximum sum of a NONEMPTY contiguous subarray of a nonempty array.
Kadane's Algorithm.approach: Best subarray ending at i either starts at i or extends the best ending at i-1. Global best is the maximum of these ending states.
Kadane's Algorithm.trace: At 4 start a fresh subarray; extend with -1,2,1 to reach 6. The -5 lowers the ending sum but does not erase global best.
Kadane's Algorithm.pitfalls: Initializing best to zero would allow an empty subarray and fail all-negative inputs. Use long sum.
Kadane's Algorithm.alternatives: Enumerate each start/end with a running sum in O(n²); recomputing each sum would be O(n³).

Next Permutation.problem: Mutate to the next lexicographic permutation. If none exists, wrap to the smallest.
Next Permutation.approach: Find the rightmost ascending pivot. Swap with the smallest greater suffix value, found from the right because the suffix is descending. Reverse the suffix to make the increase minimal.
Next Permutation.trace: [1,2,3]: pivot 2, swap with 3, suffix [2] already minimal.
Next Permutation.pitfalls: A descending array has no pivot; reverse the entire array. Equal values require >= when finding the pivot.

Majority Element-II.problem: Return all values occurring more than floor(n/3) times, sorted. At most two values qualify.
Majority Element-II.approach: Cancel triples of distinct values using two candidate counters. A value exceeding n/3 survives cancellation; recount both survivors to verify.
Majority Element-II.complexity: O(n) time; O(1) auxiliary space and at most two outputs.
Majority Element-II.trace: [1,1,1,2,2,2,3]: candidates 1,2 lose one vote to 3; actual counts both 3>2.
Majority Element-II.pitfalls: Candidate equality checks must precede empty-slot checks. Recount rather than trusting residual votes.
Majority Element-II.alternatives: HashMap frequency counting is simpler but uses O(n) space.

Find the repeating and missing number.problem: Input has n entries from [1,n], exactly one duplicate appearing twice and one missing. Return [repeating,missing].
Find the repeating and missing number.approach: Mark values in a presence array. A repeated mark detects the duplicate; an unmarked number is missing.
Find the repeating and missing number.trace: 3 is marked twice; index 4 stays unmarked.
Find the repeating and missing number.pitfalls: This simple reference does not validate every structural constraint. Sum-of-squares formulas can overflow long for large n.
Find the repeating and missing number.alternatives: XOR partitioning by a set bit separates the two anomalies in O(1) space; a final scan identifies which anomaly is repeated.

Count Inversions.problem: Count index pairs i<j with a[i]>a[j].
Count Inversions.approach: Merge sort counts pairs inside both halves recursively. For cross pairs, both halves are sorted; a monotone right pointer counts valid partners for each left value before the merge destroys half boundaries.
Count Inversions.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space including the copy; return long for pair counts.
Count Inversions.trace: For [2,4,3,5,1], reverse pairs are (4,1),(3,1),(5,1); inversions additionally include (2,1),(4,3).
Count Inversions.pitfalls: Widen to 2L*a[j] before multiplying. Negative inputs are supported. Count cross pairs before merging.
Count Inversions.alternatives: A double loop over i<j is an O(n²) reference with O(1) auxiliary space.

Reverse Pairs.problem: Count index pairs i<j with a[i]>2*a[j].
Reverse Pairs.approach: Merge sort counts pairs inside both halves recursively. For cross pairs, both halves are sorted; a monotone right pointer counts valid partners for each left value before the merge destroys half boundaries.
Reverse Pairs.complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space including the copy; return long for pair counts.
Reverse Pairs.trace: For [2,4,3,5,1], reverse pairs are (4,1),(3,1),(5,1); inversions additionally include (2,1),(4,3).
Reverse Pairs.pitfalls: Widen to 2L*a[j] before multiplying. Negative inputs are supported. Count cross pairs before merging.
Reverse Pairs.alternatives: A double loop over i<j is an O(n²) reference with O(1) auxiliary space.

Maximum Product Subarray in an Array.problem: Return the exact maximum product of a nonempty contiguous subarray.
Maximum Product Subarray in an Array.approach: Track both maximum and minimum products ending at each position. Multiplying by a negative swaps the roles of extremes; include the singleton value to allow starting over.
Maximum Product Subarray in an Array.complexity: O(n) BigInteger multiply operations; bit cost and retained storage depend on product length.
Maximum Product Subarray in an Array.trace: 2 -> hi=6 at 3 -> at -2 hi=-2,lo=-12 -> at 4 hi=4,lo=-48; best remains 6.
Maximum Product Subarray in an Array.pitfalls: Zero resets ending products. BigInteger avoids silent overflow for long products.
Maximum Product Subarray in an Array.alternatives: Enumerate all subarrays in O(n²) multiplications for a reference approach.

Merge two sorted arrays without extra sp.problem: Both arrays are sorted. Rearrange in place so conceptual a followed by b is globally sorted, keeping array lengths fixed.
Merge two sorted arrays without extra sp.approach: Compare positions separated by a shrinking ceiling-half gap in the conceptual concatenation. The gap method exploits that the two initial runs are sorted; halve until the adjacent pass completes the merge.
Merge two sorted arrays without extra sp.complexity: O((n+m) log(n+m)) time, O(1) auxiliary space.
Merge two sorted arrays without extra sp.trace: Conceptual [1,4,8,2,3,9]; gap 3 then 2 then 1 moves smaller second-run values into the first run.
Merge two sorted arrays without extra sp.pitfalls: This gap sequence is a merge technique for two sorted runs, not a general sorting guarantee for arbitrary input. Empty arrays are supported.
Merge two sorted arrays without extra sp.alternatives: Merge into a temporary array in O(n+m) time/O(n+m) space. Repeated insertion shifting uses O(nm) time and O(1) space.

Second Smallest Distinct Element.problem: Return the second DISTINCT minimum, absent if fewer than two distinct values.
Second Smallest Distinct Element.approach: Maintain the smallest two distinct processed values. A new minimum demotes the old one; a strictly intermediate value changes only second.
Second Smallest Distinct Element.trace: 4 becomes first;1 demotes4; duplicate1 does nothing;2 replaces second4.
Second Smallest Distinct Element.pitfalls: OptionalInt supports every int value without a sentinel collision.
